issues.legal_issue: An offence under another law that specifies the classes of magistrates competent to try it cannot be tried by a magistrate outside those classes, even if that magistrate has superior ordinary powers.
material_facts: The offence was created by a law that specified Magistrates of the Second or Third Class as the courts competent to try it.
The trial began before a Magistrate of the Second Class, but he was given First Class powers after recording the evidence and examining the accused, and he then delivered judgment.
The High Court set aside the convictions because the First Class Magistrate lacked jurisdiction to try the offence.
issues.conclusion: The trial by the First Class Magistrate was without jurisdiction, the proceedings were void, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 29(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, an offence under another law must be tried by the court specified in that law; the Second Schedule applies under section 29(2) only when no court is specified. The Third Schedule defines magistrates’ ordinary powers and does not confer jurisdiction contrary to a specified trial court. Section 15(2) of the Uttar Pradesh Private Forests Act specified Magistrates of the Second or Third Class. The possibility that a conviction by those magistrates would carry a right of appeal, unlike certain convictions by a First Class Magistrate, supported that reading. A trial by a magistrate not empowered to try the offence is void under section 530(p) of the Code. Jaddu v. State, A.I.R. 1952 All. 372, and Harbans Singh v. State, A.I.R. 1953 All. 179, were referred to.

predicates.criminal_trial_under_another_law: A criminal proceeding concerns an offence created by a law other than the general penal code.
predicates.governing_law_specifies_trial_courts: The law creating the offence states which classes of courts must try it.
predicates.magistrate_outside_specified_classes: The magistrate who tries the offence is not within the classes of courts specified by that law.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial under another law concerns an offence for which that law specifies the trial courts, proceedings are void if the trying magistrate is outside the specified classes.
